web_title: 8. Stage 2 Technical Structure, Institutional Flow & Momentum Setup
book_title: Chapter 8: Reading the Tape — Trend, Volume & Momentum Opportunity
question: Does the weekly and daily price structure confirm institutional accumulation, or do distribution days and a Downtrend macro regime favor waiting for support?

epigraph.quote: Never buy a stock just because it is cheap, and never ignore distribution days when the broader market is in a Downtrend. Let the pullback come to your shelf.
epigraph.author: Stan Weinstein & Mark Minervini Tape Discipline

web_blocks.html: While the broader US equity market in our November 20, 2026 ledger sits in a Downtrend (only 42.3% of stocks above their 50-day SMA, with 10 distribution days), Mondelēz is acting as a defensive Stage 2 leader [30]. At $66.28, MDLZ trades above every key moving average: +3.06% above its 10-week EMA ($64.31), +5.21% above its 50-day SMA ($63.00), +6.63% above its 30-week SMA ($62.16), and +8.64% above its 200-day SMA ($61.01).

However, the near-term tape shows two-sided institutional activity. On the positive side, daily RSI(14) is 55.97 (weekly 60.38; 4H 50.38), Bollinger Bandwidth is a tight 10.53% (STAGE2_VCP_VOLATILITY_SQUEEZE), and shares rose +0.90% on November 20 on 12.07 million shares (1.44x the 30-day average). On the cautionary side, facts_US_2026-11-20.json records 6 stock-level distribution days in the last 25 sessions alongside a -1.87% 1-week Finviz pullback and weak Confectioners industry breadth (only 20% above 50-day EMA).

web_blocks.takeaway: While MDLZ is a Stage 2 leader, 6 distribution days in 25 sessions, 20% Confectioners breadth, and a US Downtrend argue against chasing $66.28—let price pull back to the $63.35–$64.50 10W EMA/50D SMA shelf.

web_blocks.html: Our deterministic options desk check (options_snapshot.py) confirms that listed equity options do not offer superior convexity here. A representative $52.5/$77.5 call spread costs $14.10 for a $10.90 maximum gain (0.77:1 reward-to-risk, well below our 1.25:1 minimum threshold), earning a NO_OPTIONS_EDGE stamp. Direct common equity bought on a pullback to $63.35–$64.50 avoids time decay and preserves the 3.05% dividend carry.

book_paragraphs: A great business at a reasonable price can still trap your capital in dead money if you buy it right into overhead resistance during a market-wide Downtrend. That is why we always check the tape—not to predict the future with lines on a screen, but to verify whether institutional money is quietly accumulating shares or distributing them into strength.

Look at the broader US market as of November 20, 2026: our market ledger flags an active Downtrend, with only 42.3% of stocks holding above their 50-day moving average and 10 institutional distribution days on the board. Inside Mondelēz's own Confectioners industry group, only 20% of peers are holding above their 50-day EMA. Mondelēz carries a Beta of just 0.34 and is sitting near its 52-week highs—up 23.13% year-to-date—which makes it a clear relative-strength leader, yet it is not immune to tape pressure.

When we inspect the weekly, daily, and four-hour charts side by side, the primary structure is Stage 2, but the short-term volume footprint urges patience. On the weekly timeframe, Mondelēz at $66.28 trades 6.63% above a rising 30-week moving average ($62.16) and 8.64% above its 200-day moving average ($61.01), with a weekly RSI of 60.38. On the daily chart, daily RSI is a calm 55.97 and Bollinger Bandwidth has tightened to 10.53%—a classic volatility contraction pattern just 3.83% below the $68.92 52-week high. Friday's +0.90% gain came on 12.07 million shares, 1.44 times its 30-day average. At the same time, however, our facts ledger records 6 stock-level distribution days over the last 25 sessions and a -1.87% 1-week pullback.

Combining those 6 distribution days with our valuation math makes the tactical plan unmistakable. Rather than buying at $66.28 where reward-to-risk to $71.50 is only 1.08-to-1, we set our disciplined support buy zone at $63.35 to $64.50—anchored directly on the rising 10-week EMA ($64.31) and 50-day SMA ($63.00). Our hard invalidation stop at $61.43 sits just below the 30-week SMA ($62.16) and 200-day SMA ($61.01), capping risk from $64.50 at just -4.76%.

We also checked the listed options market to see if LEAPS or call spreads could juice our convexity. They cannot. Because implied volatility is modest and Mondelēz pays a 3.05% dividend that reduces call-side carry, a $52.5/$77.5 call spread costs $14.10 for only $10.90 of maximum profit—a 0.77-to-1 payoff that fails our 1.25-to-1 hurdle. When the options market gives you no edge, you wait patiently in Treasury cash for the $63.35–$64.50 common-stock shelf.

book_callouts.quote: A Stage 2 leader in a Downtrend market often gives you a second chance at its 10-week EMA before it breaks out to new highs.
book_callouts.text: Even though Friday's 1.44x volume print showed buyers stepping in at $66.28, 6 distribution days in 25 sessions and 20% industry breadth tell us supply is still overhead. Waiting for $63.35–$64.50 lets the tape prove itself.

book_subsections.title: Multi-Timeframe Anatomy: Weekly, Daily, and 4-Hour Structure
paragraphs: Let us zoom in on the exact moving-average architecture across all three timeframes so you can see why $63.35–$64.50 is such a high-probability institutional shelf. On the weekly chart (1W), Mondelēz's 30-week simple moving average sits at $62.16 and its 40-week exponential moving average sits at $61.97, both sloping upward. Right above them, the 10-week EMA sits at $64.31—representing the classic first-pullback magnet where institutional funds defend Stage 2 trends.

On the daily chart (1D), the 200-day SMA sits at $61.01, the 50-day SMA sits at $63.00, the 20-day SMA sits at $65.65, and the 10-day SMA sits at $66.66. Notice how tightly stacked those averages are: between $61.01 (200-day SMA) and $64.31 (10-week EMA), there is a dense cluster of institutional support. Meanwhile, daily ATR(14) is $1.45 (2.19% of share price), pivot S1 sits at $59.55, pivot R1 sits at $68.09, and pivot R2 sits at $71.25. On the 4-hour chart (4H), RSI sits at a neutral 50.38, showing neither oversold capitulation nor overbought exhaustion.

Why not buy immediately at $66.28? Because in a US equity market with 10 index distribution days, 42.3% breadth above the 50-day SMA, only 20% of Confectioners above their 50-day EMA, and 6 stock-level distribution days in the last 25 sessions for MDLZ itself, buying right under the $68.09–$68.92 resistance ceiling gives you poor asymmetry. Letting price digest into the $63.35–$64.50 zone aligns both the tape and the valuation. Once price tests that 10-week EMA shelf and holds on lighter selling volume, we get a much cleaner risk-reward entry with our hard stop tucked safely beneath the 30-week and 200-day moving averages at $61.43.

book_subsections.title: Why Listed Options Offer Zero Convexity Edge Here
paragraphs: Whenever we evaluate a Stage 2 setup, our options desk checks whether a bull call spread or LEAPS call can deliver better risk-adjusted convexity than common stock. For a low-beta (0.34), 3.05%-dividend consumer staple like Mondelēz, the math almost never works—and our deterministic options snapshot confirms it. A representative $52.50 / $77.50 call spread costs $14.10 per share ($1,410 per contract) for a maximum possible profit of $10.90 ($1,090 per contract), which is a 0.77-to-1 reward-to-risk ratio—well below our 1.25-to-1 minimum threshold. Worse, option holders forfeit the $2.02 annual dividend. Common stock bought patiently at $63.35–$64.50 is cleaner, cheaper, and pays you while you wait.

Even if you look at shorter-dated out-of-the-money calls around the $67.50 or $70.00 strikes, implied volatility is priced tightly against Mondelēz's 20-day realized volatility because consumer staples rarely gap 10% overnight outside of earnings. Paying theta decay while waiting for a slow-moving, 0.34-beta snacking compounder to grind through overhead resistance is a losing proposition. That is why our options playbook stamps MDLZ with NO_OPTIONS_EDGE and keeps our focus squarely on common equity limit orders in the $63.35–$64.50 support zone, where we capture both the full 3.05% dividend yield and clean 2.28-to-1 upside asymmetry without fighting expiration clocks.
